The word holograph has two separate meanings as a noun. Both are standard and accepted, but they come up in very different situations. Here's each one explained fully.
Meaning 1: A Document Written Entirely by Hand

This is the older and more legally significant meaning. A holograph is a document written completely in the handwriting of the person who authored it — not typed, not dictated to someone else, not partially handwritten. Every single word, from beginning to end, must be in the author's own hand.

Why this matters: In law, a holograph carries special weight because the handwriting itself acts as proof of who wrote it. The most common example is a holographic will — a will (a legal document telling people what to do with your belongings after you die) that someone wrote out entirely by hand themselves. In many legal systems, such a will can be valid even without witnesses, because the handwriting is considered sufficient evidence of the author's identity and intent.

Real-world examples:

  • A letter that Abraham Lincoln wrote entirely by himself, word by word, in his own hand = a holograph.
  • An original manuscript page that Charles Dickens physically wrote out himself = a holograph.
  • A will that your grandmother wrote out by hand on notebook paper = a holograph will.
  • A will that a lawyer typed and your grandmother only signed at the bottom = not a holograph, because she didn't write the body of the document.

The single most important thing to remember: a holograph means the whole document is in the author's handwriting — not just the signature, not just part of it, but all of it.
Meaning 2: A Three-Dimensional Image (the scientific meaning)

You've almost certainly heard the word hologram — those three-dimensional images that seem to float in space, like the shimmery images on credit cards or the futuristic projected images in science fiction. Holograph is sometimes used as an alternative term for the same thing.

More precisely, in scientific usage, a holograph refers to the recording itself (usually made on a special photographic plate or film using laser light) from which a three-dimensional image can be produced and viewed.

Here's what makes it different from an ordinary photograph: a regular photo captures a flat, 2D picture of something. A holograph captures information about the light waves bouncing off an object from many angles simultaneously. When you shine light through or onto the holograph, it reconstructs a full 3D image — you can shift your viewing angle and see different sides of the object, just as you would if the real object were there. It has genuine depth.

Everyday examples you may have seen:

  • The small shimmery image on a credit card or a passport — that's a basic holograph.
  • Security stickers on banknotes or software boxes that shift and appear 3D when tilted — those are holographs.
  • In science fiction (Star Wars, Iron Man, etc.), when a character projects a floating 3D image into the air — that's the concept of a holograph taken to a futuristic extreme.
How the Two Meanings Relate (and How to Tell Them Apart)

These two meanings can feel completely unrelated, and in everyday use, they mostly are. Here's the simple rule for telling them apart in context:

If you encounter holograph in a legal, historical, or archival context — discussing documents, wills, manuscripts, or letters — it means a handwritten document.

If you encounter it in a scientific, technological, or futuristic context — discussing images, optics, lasers, or security technology — it means the 3D image recording (what most people call a hologram).

One more useful distinction: in modern everyday speech, people almost always say hologram when they mean the 3D image. The word holograph in that sense appears more in technical or formal writing. So in practice, if you simply hear someone say "holograph" out loud in conversation, odds are strong they're talking about a handwritten document.
The Core Idea Behind Both Meanings

Even though the two meanings seem unrelated, they share something interesting: both have to do with something being complete and original in itself — the handwritten document is wholly in one person's hand (nothing delegated, nothing secondhand), and the holographic image captures the full three-dimensional reality of an object (not a flat, partial representation). That "wholeness" and "directness" is the thread running through both uses of the word.
